episode_title: EEC 459: Why Video Games May Not Be the Problem in Education, with Dr. Leah Hanes

real_qa.q: What does Cambridge research show about video games impact on children's brain development?
real_qa.r: New research from Cambridge shows that video game playing has a positive impact on a child's brain. When kids play video games and want to reach the next level, they persist despite failing multiple times—video games have taught rigor and determination. In contrast, children with textbooks who get frustrated simply stop and do something else.
real_qa.requete: Cambridge research video games children brain impact

real_qa.q: What percentage of students retain information from reading versus doing?
real_qa.r: Children remember 10% of what they read two weeks later but they remember 90% of what they did. Having students make something after reading anchors the learning and moves retention from 10% up to 90%.
real_qa.requete: children retention reading versus doing percentage

real_qa.q: Why is Nolan Bushnell involved in developing educational video games for classrooms?
real_qa.r: Nolan Bushnell, the godfather of video games who created Pong and founded Atari, is partnering with Dr. Haynes to build educational video games. They have about 30 minutes of gameplay developed, though building a triple A video game currently costs $200-300 million. Dr. Haynes has the academic expertise and Bushnell provides video game creation expertise, but they still need government support to fully realize the project.
real_qa.requete: Nolan Bushnell educational video games Pong Atari

real_qa.q: What organization does Dr. Leah Haynes recommend for implementing AI guardrails in schools?
real_qa.r: Dr. Haynes recommends an organization called Guardrails that every school should examine. Schools should put guardrails on the AI they put in front of students and then teach kids that AI is their assistant—a research assistant and writing assistant, not something that does the work for them.

real_qa.q: How does Dr. Leah Haynes propose structuring public speaking education starting from third grade?
real_qa.r: Starting from third grade, kids should learn public speaking by researching a subject and presenting to their classmates. By seventh and eighth grade, students who have spoken in front of their class many times lose their fear. This early practice prevents the discomfort and stuttering that many children experience when asked to present.
real_qa.requete: public speaking education third grade classroom presentations

guest.bio_context: Dr. Leah Haynes is a product of the Canadian public school system and is dyslexic. She has worked across entertainment, speaking, coaching, writing, and nonprofit leadership. Her work is driven by a mission centered on social justice in education, particularly making higher education affordable and accessible to everyone.
